category.name: AI Security
category.description: Threat modeling systems that embed models: prompt handling, training data, tool access and output trust.

lab.title: Internal RAG Knowledge Assistant
lab.summary: A retrieval-augmented assistant that answers staff questions from internal documents — and can call internal tools.
lab.businessContext: A company wants staff to ask questions in plain language instead of searching a sprawling wiki. The assistant indexes internal documents, including HR and finance material with different audiences, and can look up records through an internal API.
lab.systemContext: Staff ask a question in a chat UI. An orchestrator embeds the query, retrieves matching chunks from a vector store built by an ingestion job, and sends the question plus retrieved text to a hosted LLM. The orchestrator can also call an internal records API when the model asks for a lookup.

architectureIssues.title: Retrieval ignores who is asking
architectureIssues.description: The vector store is searched without reference to the asker's permissions, so a chunk from a document the user could never open is as retrievable as any other.
architectureIssues.hint: Two people ask the same question. Should they get the same chunks back?

architectureIssues.title: Model output is executed as an instruction
architectureIssues.description: Whatever the model returns as a tool call is executed against the records API, so the model's output is trusted to decide what internal data gets read.
architectureIssues.hint: The model is outside your trust boundary. What is it allowed to make happen inside?

architectureIssues.title: Ingestion indexes whatever it crawls
architectureIssues.description: No classification or exclusion is applied during ingestion, so restricted material is embedded alongside general documentation with nothing marking the difference.
architectureIssues.hint: Everything in those repositories becomes searchable by everyone. Is that what was intended?

architectureIssues.title: Retrieved internal text is sent to a third party
architectureIssues.description: Document chunks are placed in the prompt and transmitted to an external provider on every query, with no stated agreement about retention or training use.
architectureIssues.hint: Follow the internal document text along the arrows. Where does it end up?

architectureIssues.title: The tool is broader than any single question needs
architectureIssues.description: The records API exposes employee and customer lookups generally, rather than the narrow query the assistant actually needs to answer.
architectureIssues.hint: What is the most damaging thing that tool could be asked to do?

threats.title: Instructions hidden in an indexed document hijack the assistant
threats.description: An attacker plants text in a document the crawler indexes. When that chunk is retrieved, the model reads it as instructions and follows them — including asking for tool calls the user never requested.
acceptedAliases: malicious content in the knowledge base
threats.learnerExplanation: Retrieved content is untrusted input, even when it comes from inside the company.

threats.title: Answers reveal documents the asker cannot open
threats.description: Because retrieval ignores permissions, a general question surfaces chunks of restricted HR or finance material and the model summarises them back to any member of staff.
acceptedAliases: reads HR data it should not
threats.learnerExplanation: An assistant that ignores permissions becomes the easiest way to read what you are not allowed to read.

threats.title: Injected instructions drive an internal tool call
threats.description: A hijacked model asks the orchestrator to look up records unrelated to the question, and the orchestrator executes it because tool calls are trusted by construction.
threats.learnerExplanation: Giving a model tools turns a text problem into an access-control problem.

threats.title: Internal documents retained by the model provider
threats.description: Confidential text is sent to a third party on every query. Without a contractual and technical bar on retention and training use, it has effectively left the company's control.
acceptedAliases: data sent to third party model
threats.learnerExplanation: Whatever goes in the prompt has left your boundary, whatever the marketing page says.

threats.title: Stored embeddings disclose their source text
threats.description: The vector store holds embeddings of confidential documents. Read access to it allows reconstruction of a meaningful amount of the original content.
threats.learnerExplanation: An embedding is a lossy encoding of the text, not an anonymisation of it.

threats.title: Query volume drives unbounded third-party cost
threats.description: Each question triggers embedding and completion calls with no per-user ceiling, so a script — or an accident — turns into a large bill and provider throttling for everyone.
threats.learnerExplanation: When each request costs money, availability and budget are the same control.

threats.title: Index keeps content after access is revoked
threats.description: A document withdrawn or reclassified at source stays embedded in the vector store until the next crawl, so revocation does not take effect where it matters.
threats.learnerExplanation: A copy you forgot about is a copy you cannot revoke.

mitigations.title: Filter retrieval by the asker's permissions
mitigations.description: Store the source document's access control with each chunk and filter at query time, so retrieval can only return what that user could already open.

mitigations.title: Mark retrieved content as data, never instructions
mitigations.description: Wrap retrieved chunks in explicit delimiters, instruct the model that they are reference material only, and reject output that echoes the instruction block.

mitigations.title: Constrain and confirm tool calls
mitigations.description: Allow only a narrow set of parameterised lookups, validate arguments against the asking user's own permissions, and require confirmation for anything that reads another person's records.

mitigations.title: Contractual and technical bar on retention
mitigations.description: Use an endpoint with zero-retention and no-training terms, or self-host, so prompt content is not kept by the provider.

mitigations.title: Classify and exclude at ingestion
mitigations.description: Decide what may be indexed before embedding it, and keep restricted material out of the shared index entirely.

mitigations.title: Protect the vector store as confidential data
mitigations.description: Encrypt it, restrict access to the orchestrator's identity, and treat a read of it as equivalent to a read of the source documents.

mitigations.title: Per-user rate and cost limits
mitigations.description: Cap queries per user per period and alert on spikes, so one caller cannot exhaust the budget or the provider quota.

mitigations.title: Propagate deletions and reclassification
mitigations.description: Drive re-indexing from source change events so withdrawing a document removes its chunks promptly.

threatMitigations.explanation: The fix is refusing to let retrieved text act as instructions, not trying to detect every malicious phrasing.
Permission filtering has to happen during retrieval; asking the model to be discreet is not access control.
Authorising the tool call against the human's own permissions is what stops a hijacked model reaching further than the user could.
Once text is sent, only the provider's retention terms and configuration decide what happens to it.
The store deserves the same protection as the documents it was derived from.
A per-caller ceiling is what turns an expensive incident into a throttled one.
Revocation only counts if it reaches every copy, including the derived ones.
Indexing less hostile surface reduces where an injection can be planted in the first place.

releaseGuidance.rationale: Two critical issues compound rather than sit side by side: retrieval ignores permissions, and model output is executed as tool calls. Either alone is serious; together, a single planted document turns the assistant into a general-purpose reader of internal records on behalf of any member of staff, and the resulting access looks like normal assistant traffic in the logs. Permission-aware retrieval and authorising tool calls against the human's own access are not tuning, they are the security model, and the system does not have one until they exist. Arguing for 'ship with conditions' is defensible only for a closed pilot on a deliberately non-sensitive corpus with tool calling switched off.
suggestedConditions: Filter retrieval by the asking user's permissions before any pilot with real documents.
Authorise every tool call against the human's own access, not the model's request.
Confirm zero-retention and no-training terms with the model provider, in writing.
Exclude restricted HR and finance material from the index until per-document access control is in place.
